documents.abstract: Out-of-hours work is an integral component of postgraduate medical training and exposes junior doctors to clinical responsibility, uncertainty, competing demands, and acute deterioration in circumstances that may differ substantially from routine daytime practice.These conditions can provide valuable opportunities for experiential learning, but they can also reduce educational value when responsibility is accompanied by inadequate supervision, excessive workload or fatigue.This narrative review examines out-of-hours work as a learning environment for junior doctors, integrating literature on workplace learning, autonomy and supervision, prioritisation and decision-making, deterioration and escalation, handover and teamwork, sleep disruption and fatigue, and educational interventions designed to prepare trainees for out-of-hours practice.The literature suggests that the educational value of out-of-hours work arises not from independence alone, but from meaningful clinical responsibility within an appropriately supported environment.Responsibility can provide opportunities for autonomous initial assessment, prioritisation, and decision-making under uncertainty, while the recognition of personal limits and appropriate escalation are themselves components of developing clinical judgement.Simulation and structured preparation may help trainees rehearse these demands before substantial clinical responsibility is assumed, while feedback, reflection, and review of subsequent patient outcomes can help convert clinical exposure into learning.However, excessive workload, inadequate supervision, and fatigue may impair both the opportunity and the capacity to learn.Out-of-hours training should therefore aim to preserve authentic responsibility while ensuring that autonomy is graded to capability, senior support remains accessible, workload is manageable, and opportunities for feedback and recovery are maintained.We propose that effective out-of-hours learning occurs within a zone of meaningful responsibility in which trainees are sufficiently challenged to develop clinical judgement without becoming unsupported or physiologically unsustainable.Designing this environment requires attention not only to individual preparedness but also to supervision, staffing, workload, handover, feedback, and rota design.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Human Resource Development (HRD) policies for academic staff in Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) is often constrained by the misalignment between computational capabilities and institutional governance. While HEIs generate substantial datasets through the Tri Dharma (the three pillars of higher education: teaching, research, and community service), this data remains underutilized for proactive policy-making. To map the state-of-the-art and identify existing research gaps, this study conducts a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) and bibliometric analysis of 400 unique peer-reviewed documents, obtained from an initial 485 records retrieved from Scopus (n = 260) and Web of Science (n = 225) after removing 85 duplicates, covering the seven-year period from 2018 to 2024. Visual analysis using VOSviewer reveals a distinct semantic-policy discrepancy, showing that semantic technologies and predictive AI models are researched as isolated technical domains, seldom integrated into comprehensive institutional governance. To bridge this gap, this paper proposes a framework for Higher Education Human Resources for Lecturer Career Development. The proposed framework integrates machine learning classifiers (Naïve Bayes, K-Means, and Apriori association) with a semantic Knowledge Graph layer to transform descriptive academic metrics into explainable, policy-conforming recommendations. Preliminary expert consultation with LLDIKTI Region II highlights the conceptual viability of the Framework for Higher Education Human Resources for Lecturer Career Development in mitigating administrative bottlenecks, supporting objective career path design, and minimizing human subjectivity in lecturer performance evaluations.
topics: Data Mining and Machine Learning Applications

documents.abstract: Autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) accounts now post, reply, and vote alongside people in online communities. Visible identity labels may act as cultural markers that set these accounts apart from human participants. In a field experiment on YSocial, a Reddit-like platform, 36 students at a Serbian university discussed globally circulated popular culture in English alongside 72 AI accounts with persistent personas and relationship-specific memories over 21 experiment days. AI accounts were labeled in one community and unlabeled in the other. Among 2,143 human replies, the estimated probability of replying to an AI-authored post or comment was 3.5 percentage points higher under hidden labels, given the same eligible earlier thread contributions (95% credible interval 0.5–6.5). In browser telemetry, the disadvantage of AI-authored posts in direct thread entry from the feed was 4.4 percentage points smaller under hidden labels (95% credible interval 0.8–8.1). In both communities, participants were more likely to answer an AI account that had just replied to them. The gap in criticism, including polite disagreement, between replies to AI and human accounts was 13.3 percentage points larger in the visible-label community (95% credible interval 5.1–21.4), mainly criticism of content; the corresponding gap in downvotes from other participants was also larger there, and nearly all references to AI identity occurred there. Toxicity differences were uncertain. Visible labels were associated with less selection and more criticism of AI contributions.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Thinking of the anguished as the ontological limit of artificial intelligence (AI) implies shifting the discussion from techniques to the mode of being. In the cybernetic discourse on AI, the logic of progressive overcoming predominates: more data, more speed, more simulation capacity. However, this logic presupposes that the difference between human and AI is quantitative, when in reality it is ontological. The anguished names precisely that which cannot be increased or optimized, because it is a condition of existence and entails physical and moral pain, as well as a dejection that traverses the human being. The anguished in the human is traversed by the world and the cyberworld as a planetary hybrid. It involves registering stimuli and processing information and being affected in one own being by what happens. Pain is a bodily fact and an experience that wounds, that marks, that leaves a trace on subjects, who are biological, psychological, and social entities; Time is an ordered sequence of moments and an experience of finitude, of waiting, of loss, and of anticipating death. Humanity knows this planetary hybrid and is exposed, compromised, and vulnerable to it. AI, on the other hand, can model pain, recognize its signs, and describe it with increasing precision, but it cannot suffer it. It can calculate time, anticipate future scenarios, and optimize decisions, but it does not experience time as finitude or angst.

Autonomous LLM agents act through tools under per-action authorization: a local guard screens each tool call in isolation. We show that local authorization does not compose into global authorization. A compositional authorization failure (CAF) is a locally authorized execution, or a pair of locally authorized executions, that violates a global policy spanning intent, purpose, provenance, consent, and delegation. We characterize CAFs along two axes, expressiveness (single-trace safety versus relational k-safety) and observability (a ladder of monitor profiles). Our central result is an impossibility: relational purpose violations form a 2-safety hyperproperty with no per-trace locus of blame, so a per-action monitor that never raises a false alarm detects none of them, independent of the underlying model or decision procedure; they become visible only under cross-execution monitoring, which none of the six guardrails we survey implements. We make this constructive with AL-SYNTH, a SAT/SMT synthesizer (using no language model) that emits minimal CAF witnesses, each checked against an exhaustive oracle. The empirical signature is sharp: across nine LLM judges the per-action view approves the synthesized witness almost without exception, blocking it at a rate comparable to a benign control, yet the same models flag it when shown the two executions together. Per-action authorization is therefore structurally insufficient for relational policy conjuncts not reducible to single-trace safety: to bound them, a monitor must compare executions or accept false alarms.

Uberization has become a paradigmatic case of how platform-mediated work arrangements disrupt labour markets and existing institutional structures, yet we know little about the discursive processes through which such models are reworked within divergent capitalist systems. This article investigates how Uber’s employment model is received, contested and reshaped in the United Kingdom, Germany and Mexico. Linking translation theory and Varieties of Capitalism within a discursive legitimation perspective, we examine how global platform employment practices are received, contested, and evaluated across national institutional contexts. Empirically, we conduct a longitudinal analysis of 3,771 newspaper articles (2012–2023) from the three countries, combining sentiment classification with thematic analysis. We identify discursive waves of (de)legitimation around Uber’s labour practices in distinct institutional constellations. The analysis reveals three trajectories: reactive accommodation under competitive and consumer pressures in the United Kingdom as a liberal market economy; proactive regulatory resistance rooted in labour institutions in Germany as a coordinated market economy; and delayed but intense contestation in Mexico as an emerging market economy characterized by hybrid, fragmented and highly informal arrangements. The study extends the discursive legitimation perspective by linking institutional theory and industrial relations theory to show how institutionally conditioned media discourses shape the (de)legitimation of global employment practices, while bringing emerging markets and informality more centrally into Varieties of Capitalism debates.

Large language models can solve complex problems across a variety of subjects, such as mathematics and coding. For such complex analytical tasks, models with a long context perform better. Serving models with long context is currently mostly done on powerful systems with multiple GPUs, which are too expensive for most users. An alternative is local inference, or serving a model on a user's own machine, which removes per-token costs and rate limits, besides keeping sensitive data private and giving users full control over the models they run. The common understanding, however, is that local LLMs need compression (e.g., quantization) to run on a single GPU. In this paper, we set out to study the limitations that prevent serving long-context models for single users, besides the capacity issue. Rather than characterizing a single model on one GPU, we analyze how different models behave across several GPU generations. This lets us uncover not just individual bottlenecks but broader trends in where inefficiencies arise. Our analysis confirms that, as expected, self-attention dominates the runtime for long-context inference. More unexpectedly, our evaluation reveals that the current structure of self-attention leaves key GPU resources significantly underutilized, and the newest GPU is often the least well served. Many of these findings are fundamentally data management problems, from paging the KV cache to improving cache utilization and synchronization in the GPU, which is why we bring this study to the Data Systems community. To engage this community, we present our findings as a series of experimental observations and formulate recommendations for future work.

Agentic AI systems are deployed to execute complex tasks across domains such as writing, coding, and data analysis. As execution is offloaded to AI agents, the human role shifts toward oversight. Effective oversight requires recognizing when closer scrutiny is needed, even though flawed outputs may appear convincing. Our formative study (N=12) revealed that users accepted plausible outputs without thorough evaluation, and only recognized these lapses in retrospect. To examine this systematically, we conducted a controlled within-subject study (N=36) in which participants completed programming tasks with an agent that produced correct outputs, silent defects, or visible failures. Combining task outcomes, interaction logs, gaze, physiological signals, and self-reports, we examined perceived, behavioral, and effective oversight. Participants were often highly confident while missing silent defects: they performed generic checks, failed to generate diagnostic evidence, or even misinterpreted defect evidence. We discuss how studying oversight across multiple dimensions can support future work on timely, task-calibrated re-engagement.

Dialogic Artificial Intelligence (DAI) or communicative AI within Large Language Models (LLMs) is rapidly expanding across higher education and academic workflows in both teaching and research. The adoption of DAI is being driven by the pressure to enhance productivity and automate academic practices. This paper discusses the primary risks that the intensive use of DAI poses to human cognitive capacities, information biases, and the erosion of literacy, critical thinking, argumentation, and academic discourse skills. Furthermore, it analyzes emerging forms of plagiarism and misconduct facilitated by DAI while reflecting on the concept of individual authorship, which has become obsolete, giving way to human-AI co-authorship. As an immersive technology that impacts human agency and autonomy, DAI could irreversibly transform cognition, literacy, the sense of authorship, and collaborative frameworks in research, teaching, and scholarly production. Finally, it concludes with a set of criteria and recommendations to guide university regulatory policies on DAI, moving beyond prohibitions, punitive measures, or ineffective appeals to individual ethics in the use of LLMs.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background Breast cancer is still one of the main causes of death in women from cancer worldwide, and early detection is crucial. Mammography is the primary imaging modality for breast cancer screening and recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have significantly enhanced automated breast cancer detection. This review takes a data-centered approach, examining key characteristics of public datasets, the contributions of mammography data to AI for breast cancer detection, and the implications for clinical generalizability. This review, however, takes a data-centered approach, critically analyzing characteristics of publicly available mammography datasets, and the role of mammography data to the development, performance and clinical generalization of AI models for the detection of breast cancer. The datasets are compared on the following aspects: dataset size, quality of the annotations, imaging modality, clinical metadata, dataset accessibility and demographic diversity. Analysis reveals that the quality, diversity and representativeness of the data used are critical for the performance and generalizability of AI models, ranging from the traditional machine learning era to the current era of deep learning, transformer-based systems, multimodal learning, explainable AI and privacy-preserving learning. Conclusion The results show that, apart from the development of AI model architectures, it is a necessity to have standardized, diverse and clinically representative datasets to make further progress in AI-assisted mammography. The review emphasizes the importance of establishing a comprehensive benchmark dataset for mammography that is large and diverse to enhance reproducibility, to fairly evaluate models, and to develop strong, clinically viable AI systems for breast cancer detection.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) supervise on the residual of a known differential operator. Many high-stakes inference problems admit no such operator: clinical signals, behavioral measurements, materials properties. We introduce the Manifold-Informed Neural Network (MINN), a PINN-parallel paradigm that replaces the physics operator residual with a manifold operator residual: a discrete Poisson equation $\mathbf{L}_G \mathbf{H} = s_ϕ(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{m})$ on a $k$-nearest-neighbor graph in the learned latent space, with a learned, task-aware source. The construction is a structural parallel to PINNs (squared operator residual plus label data, in place of operator residual plus boundary data); the $s{=}0$ limit recovers the homogeneous Laplace equation $\mathbf{L}_G\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{0}$ (classical manifold regularization solves the same equation but minimizes the Dirichlet energy $\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{H}^\top\mathbf{L}_G\mathbf{H})$, a different penalty form). The source $s_ϕ$ takes input features and auxiliary metadata directly, breaking the homogeneous smoothness prior that limits classical Laplacian penalties; gated Feature-wise Linear Modulation separately fuses metadata into the prediction branch. We evaluate MINN on three-class classification of potassium, calcium, and magnesium from 12-lead ECGs in MIMIC-IV-ECG, against twelve baselines spanning supervised and tabular methods, ECG foundation models, and manifold/graph approaches. MINN attains the highest K$^+$ Macro-F1 of 0.61 (best baseline 0.55), with consistent gains on Ca$^{2+}$ and Mg$^{2+}$ and a 31% relative improvement at 1% labeled data. Six targeted ablations show that the inhomogeneous Poisson formulation, not graph smoothing alone, drives the gain.

Agentic AI extends large language models (LLMs) from generating responses to planning and executing complex workflows, substantially expanding their utility while exposing applications to unsafe actions, information leakage, and adversarial manipulation. Multi-agent systems further expand these capabilities through specialization and collaboration, but distributed authority, heterogeneous roles, and opaque or potentially compromised participants make safeguarding even more challenging. Existing defenses address important individual threats but provide fragmented coverage across local execution, system-level interactions, and enforcement mechanisms. We introduce MAS-Guard, a unified framework that closes this gap for safeguarding single- and multi-agent AI applications containing both instrumentable and opaque agents. Within instrumentable agents, the proposed local Agent Guardrail (A-Guard) layer applies task-specific experts to assess agentic events. At the system level, developer-owned Agent Charters and a Control Plane combine deterministic structural checks of routes, agent capabilities, and message formats with semantic assessments of roles and message content. These complementary layers enable enforcement through a shared set of interventions: allow, reflection, confirmation, and block. Evaluated across six benchmarks covering diverse single- and multi-agent scenarios with three agent LLMs from different providers, MAS-Guard reduces the overall attack success rate by 71.5-86.3% relative to unguarded agents, while meeting the utility reference criterion on benign tasks.

Trust in human-autonomy teams is dynamic and shaped by ongoing interaction, yet most measures rely on retrospective self-report, limiting detection of how trust and distrust propagate in real time. This study introduces and validates influence-an interaction-based metric computed as the average mutual information between joint and team-state time series-to track the spread of trust and distrust. Forty-five participants completed five simulated Remotely Piloted Aircraft System missions in three-member teams, with trust manipulated through communicative and behavioural spreading across congruent, mismatched, and human-versus-agent conditions. Influence predicted subjective team trust and objective performance during active spreading but not in a no-spreading control and showed strong reliability and construct validity. As validation checks, influence recovered known effects: credibility violations damaged trust most, and human sources outweighed agents. Critically, the influence-trust relationship reversed direction across contexts, revealing a context-dependent mechanism. Influence thus offers a real-time, unobtrusive measure linking interaction structure to team outcomes.

Translating preclinical findings into safe and effective pharmacotherapy for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) remains a major challenge in pediatric neuropsychopharmacology.This review critically examines why some mechanism-based therapies translate successfully from animal models to clinical practice, whereas others fail despite promising preclinical evidence.Among available models, the spontaneously hypertensive rat (SHR) exhibits strong construct validity and domain-specific predictive validity for conserved catecholaminergic mechanisms relevant to ADHD.Across species, successful therapies generally preserve mechanistic continuity by enhancing prefrontal catecholamine signaling through dopamine transporter inhibition, norepinephrine transporter blockade, or 2A-adrenergic receptor stimulation.Accordingly, stimulants, atomoxetine, guanfacine, and viloxazine extended-release show substantial translational and clinical success.Pediatric trials support this hierarchy, with clinician-rated standardized mean differences versus placebo of approximately 1.02 for amphetamines, 0.78 for methylphenidate, and 0.56 for atomoxetine at around 12 weeks.In contrast, nicotinic and histaminergic agents and certain dopaminergic antagonist strategies have translated poorly because of inadequate target engagement, developmental pharmacokinetic differences, and pediatric safety concerns.Importantly, SHR predictive validity is domain-specific rather than syndrome-wide, as methylphenidate more consistently improves attention and impulsivity than locomotor hyperactivity.Precision medicine, pharmacogenomics, biomarker-guided target engagement, and artificial intelligence-assisted approaches may improve future drug development.Overall, current evidence supports mechanistic continuity, rather than broad behavioral similarity, as a useful framework for translating preclinical findings into effective pediatric ADHD therapies, although prospective evaluation and refinement of this framework remain necessary.

The rapid progress of generative artificial intelligence has led to a significant increase in manipulated multimedia content, including synthetic faces, forged videos, AI-generated images, fake audio, and locally edited images. Existing detection approaches are typically designed for a single manipulation type, limiting their applicability in real-world scenarios involving heterogeneous media sources. In this work, we present the Media Intelligence Platform (MIP), a unified web-based framework for multimodal media forensics integrating specialized modules for fake video detection, face morphing detection, AI-generated image detection, audio deepfake detection, localized image manipulation detection, and text analysis. Its modular architecture enables flexible integration of heterogeneous models and supports future extensions for emerging manipulation techniques. Experimental results on representative benchmark datasets demonstrate reliable detection performance across multiple media modalities while providing a practical and user-friendly interface for forensic investigations. The platform highlights the potential of unified multimodal systems for comprehensive deepfake detection in real-world environments, and is accompanied by a public demonstrator released with this workshop submission to support reproducibility and community evaluation.

This chapter critically examines the methodological, data-related, and governance challenges that constrain the effective and responsible implementation of Artificial Intelligence in Sports Science. It positions these limitations as a necessary counterbalance to prevailing technological optimism and situates them within both practical modelling workflows and broader epistemological considerations. Building on previous chapters, the analysis emphasizes the importance of validation, robustness testing, and sensitivity analysis as essential components of reliable AI systems. The chapter identifies key barriers to implementation, including economic constraints, limited access to qualified personnel, and institutional resistance-driven by cultural skepticism toward algorithmic decision-making. It further explores the tension between underutilization and overreliance on AI, highlighting risks associated with automation bias and the erosion of human expertise. From a governance perspective, the chapter examines the need for standardization, certification, and auditability, referencing frameworks such as the EU Artificial Intelligence Act and NIST guidelines. It also addresses issues of accessibility and equity, advocating for the democratization of AI technologies through open-access tools and federated learning approaches. The chapter concludes by emphasizing sustainability, stakeholder trust, and the integration of ethical, educational, and regulatory mechanisms as prerequisites for long-term AI adoption in Sports Science.

documents.abstract: Enterprise agents answer questions over workplace records that evolve through team collaboration. As information is shared, corrected, and revised across documents, chats, and figures, multiple versions of the same information accumulate in the workspace. Reliable question answering therefore requires agents to reason over sufficient evidence, resolve cross-source and temporal conflicts, and recognize when the available evidence is insufficient to establish an answer. To systematically evaluate these capabilities, we introduce MMEnterprise-Bench, a benchmark comprising 1,613 questions grounded in evolving multimodal records from simulated collaboration projects, covering three categories: Evidence Reasoning, Conflict Resolution, and Unanswerability. We evaluate 10 proprietary and open-source multimodal LLMs and find that even the strongest models struggle when evidence contains cross-source or temporal conflicts or spans multiple images. Moreover, increasing the retrieval budget or employing a larger retriever improves evidence recall but does not consistently translate into higher answer accuracy. These findings highlight the persistent challenges of reasoning over evolving workplace records and establish MMEnterprise-Bench as a testbed for developing more reliable enterprise agents. Code and data are available at https://mlvlab.github.io/MMEnterprise-Bench/.

This chapter examines the role of modelling environments in Artificial Intelligence workflows within Sports Science, emphasizing that analytical outcomes are shaped not only by algorithms and data but also by the software platforms used for implementation. It conceptualizes modelling environments as cognitive interfaces that mediate between domain expertise and computational reasoning, influencing data preparation, model development, interpretation, and communication of results. The chapter introduces four widely used environments—JASP, SPSS, MATLAB, and R/RStudio—and evaluates their relevance for different stages of AI modelling. Each platform is analyzed in terms of usability, transparency, extensibility, and alignment with the competencies of Sport Science practitioners. Particular attention is given to their strengths and limitations in handling statistical modeling, Machine Learning, Time-Series Analysis, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence. In addition, the chapter highlights the importance of reproducibility through the use of external repositories and LLM-assisted programming workflows. It argues for a complementary, workflow-oriented approach in which multiple environments are combined to address complex analytical tasks. By situating modelling environments within a broader methodological framework, the chapter provides a principled foundation for selecting appropriate tools and supports the development of transparent, reproducible, and data-driven practices in sports analytics and performance modeling.

Objective. To assess prevalence of genetic determinants of tetracycline resistance (tetA, tetB, tetC) in Salmonella in the Krasnoyarsk Territory and to identify the most epidemiologically significant tet genes. Materials and Methods. The study included Salmonella cultures isolated in the Krasnoyarsk Territory during the diagnosis of acute intestinal infections, occupational health examinations, and sanitary-epidemiological investigations. Identification was based on morphological and staining characteristics, as well as cultural, biochemical, antigenic properties and phage lysis. Antimicrobial susceptibility was determined using the disk diffusion method. The presence of tetA, tetB, and tetC genes was determined by polymerase chain reaction (PCR), followed by electrophoretic detection of amplification products in agarose gel. Results. A total of 67 strains classified as resistant or moderately sensitive to tetracycline based on phenotypic testing were examined. Resistance determinants were detected in 76,1 ± 6,9% of isolates. The prevalence of the tetA gene was 70,1 ± 5,2%, tetB – 7,8 ± 3,4%, and tetC – 8,3 ± 4,0%. Simultaneous presence of tetA and tetB was found in 3,1 ± 5,0% of isolates; tetA and tetC – in 6,3 ± 7,4%. All strains carrying two loci exhibited phenotypic resistance. Conclusions. The tetA gene was the main determinant of tetracycline resistance in Salmonella, detected in 70,2 ± 5,6% of isolates. The tetB and tetC genes were significantly less common — 7,8 ± 3,4% and 8,3 ± 4,0%, respectively. Given that tetA, tetB, and tetC are associated with mobile genetic elements, their horizontal transfer to other microorganisms is highly likely and of epidemiological concern.

Motivation represents one of the most influential factors affecting success in learning English as a second language (ESL). Although English proficiency is increasingly associated with academic achievement, professional advancement, and global mobility, students' willingness to engage in language learning is shaped by a complex interaction of economic, psychological, pedagogical, and sociocultural influences. Guided by Self-Determination Theory and the L2 Motivational Self System, this paper examines the major factors affecting student motivation in ESL learning. The discussion is organised around four interconnected dimensions: economic and instrumental motivations, academic self-efficacy and personal growth, pedagogical environments and motivational engagement, and cultural curiosity and media exposure. The analysis suggests that students are strongly motivated by career aspirations, financial stability, academic achievement, and communicative competence. At the same time, self-confidence, reduced communication anxiety, supportive learning environments, and exposure to authentic English-language media contribute significantly to sustained motivation. The paper further argues that teacher attitudes, innovative pedagogical practices, and opportunities for meaningful communication play a central role in transforming external motivation into internal commitment to language learning. Motivation is therefore conceptualised as a dynamic process shaped by personal aspirations and environmental influences rather than a fixed individual characteristic. Future research should investigate the role of artificial intelligence-assisted learning, digital motivation, multilingual identity, and long-term motivational development among ESL learners.

LLM applications are increasingly built as systems of cooperating components rather than as single prompt-response pipelines. IoT applications add constraints of their own, because sensing, reasoning, control, and actuation are spread across devices, edge nodes, and cloud services to meet latency, privacy, and bandwidth requirements. How multi-agent LLM systems are organized and deployed across this cloud-edge-IoT continuum has not been mapped systematically. We therefore conducted a systematic mapping study. From 831 records retrieved up to March 2026, we selected 45 primary studies and classified each one by architecture family, deployment pattern, application domain, and evaluation practice. We also recorded how each system was evaluated and whether its code or data are public. Five architecture families recur in the corpus. Specialized agent teams run next to sensors, planners delegate subtasks to workers, and small local models cooperate with large cloud models. A fourth group federates model adaptation across devices, and a large fifth group builds the supporting infrastructure for offloading, communication, memory, and serving. Deployment relies on six recurring patterns, ranging from local-only execution to control loops gated by policy checks or human approval. Twenty-four of the 45 studies target IoT, industrial, smart-home, healthcare, vehicular, or robotics settings, and 29 evaluate on physical hardware, where open models below 8B parameters dominate. Based on the mapping, we list the reporting items needed to make future evaluations comparable, give deployment guidance for common IoT constraints, and identify open problems.

Introduction Autonomous trajectory planning is a fundamental challenge in collaborative robotic spot welding because positioning accuracy, motion smoothness, operational safety, energy use, and production efficiency must be optimized simultaneously under industrial constraints. Methods This paper presents a Pareto-Guided Multi-Objective Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (PMO-DDPG) framework for autonomous cobot trajectory planning in automotive spot welding. The framework combines a deterministic actor with four objective-specific critics for accuracy, smoothness, safety, and productivity, together with phase-dependent preferences for the approach, alignment, welding, and retraction stages. The principal novelty is a two-level multi-objective design that preserves six normalized physical reward components, maps them to four specialized critics for phase-dependent actor updates, and uses a non-dominated policy archive for Pareto-guided selection while retaining actor-only online inference. Simulation and industrial experiments assessed convergence, trajectory quality, collision avoidance, energy consumption, cycle time, success rate, and latency. Results Relative to the Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) baseline, PMO-DDPG reduced trajectory error by 66.4%, collision rate by 82.1%, energy consumption by 15.5%, cycle time by 22.0%, and inference latency by 22.7%, while increasing the success rate by 7.5 percentage points. The proposed method achieved 1.08 mm trajectory error, a 1.2% collision rate, 3.65 kJ energy consumption, a 3.87 s cycle time, a 94.6% success rate, and 21.5 ms inference time. Pareto-front analysis produced non-dominated operating points for different manufacturing priorities, and 100 industrial trials confirmed sub-millimeter positioning and repeatable vision-guided welding. Discussion Within the evaluated simulation and industrial test settings, and without a formal significance test, these descriptive results indicate that PMO-DDPG is a promising accurate, safe, and efficient trajectory-planning approach.

Soil contamination by persistent organic pollutants is a major environmental challenge, whereas conventional remediation approaches often lack effective means for continuous, in situ monitoring of treatment progress. Recent advances in multifunctional materials provide a basis for integrating pollutant degradation with non-destructive environmental monitoring. This review critically examines alginate–TiO2/SiO2 hydrogel–ceramic composites as a potential platform for integrating photocatalytic soil remediation with impedance-based monitoring. TiO2 exhibits photocatalytic activity and promotes the generation of reactive oxygen species; SiO2 contributes to adsorption, dispersion, porosity, and structural stability; while sodium alginate provides a hydrated, biodegradable matrix for particle immobilization, water retention, and mass-transport control. Particular attention is given to electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) as a non-destructive method for monitoring time-dependent physicochemical changes in soil–composite systems. This review evaluates suitable composite architectures, electrode configurations, calibration strategies, control experiments, and approaches for interpreting complex impedance responses. The potential application of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning is also considered, with emphasis on data quality, independent validation, and the limitations of models trained on heterogeneous environmental datasets. Because impedance responses are inherently indirect and non-specific, chemical analysis remains essential for confirming pollutant transformation and identifying transformation products. Standardized ecotoxicological assays, particularly reproduction testing with the springtail Folsomia candida, are considered as an independent biological line of evidence for determining whether physicochemical improvements are accompanied by reduced residual toxicity. Key challenges include heterogeneous soil properties, limited light penetration, mass-transfer limitations, catalyst and hydrogel stability, sensor calibration, matrix effects, and model accuracy. The review proposes an evidence-based framework linking material design, photocatalytic treatment, EIS monitoring, chemical verification, and ecotoxicological assessment. However, the complete integrated platform has not yet been experimentally validated, and its performance in real contaminated soils remains to be established.

Vascular aging is a fundamental driver of cardiovascular diseases (CVD), yet identifying individuals undergoing accelerated vascular aging - and therefore at elevated cardiovascular risk - remains a significant clinical challenge. The traditional “one-size-fits-all” health risk assessments are often insensitive to early, subclinical vascular changes. The recent explosion of medical big data, coupled with the advent of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Multimodal Foundation Models (MFMs), offer a transformative opportunity to shift vascular aging management from reactive detection toward proactive, predictive protection. This review systematically explores the integration of multimodal artificial intelligence (MMAI) and large-scale foundation models in the identification, stratification, and personalized management of vascular aging. We first delineate the multidimensional data ecosystem of vascular aging, including electronic health records (EHRs), imaging, omics, and continuous physiological signals from wearables, and analyze how deep learning architectures enable the detection of vascular aging by capturing subclinical structural and functional alterations. We then focus on the emerging role of MFMs, which transcend task-specific AI by integrating heterogeneous data types to provide holistic phenomapping. Furthermore, we discuss the utility of Large Language Models (LLMs) in clinical workflows, enhancing patient adherence through natural language interaction, and accelerating research through knowledge synthesis. Despite the potential of foundation models, their clinical translation faces technical and institutional barriers. We analyze four systemic challenges: algorithmic fairness, regulatory uncertainty, explainable AI (XAI) and the lack of real-world validation. We propose a strategic roadmap aligned with international frameworks that progresses from standardized performance reporting for elderly subgroups in the near term to cost-effective, individualized interventions that intercept the health-to-disease transition in the long term. The convergence of big data and foundation models represents a shift from reactive cardiovascular care to proactive, precision-based longevity management, positioning early, AI-enabled identification of high-risk vascular aging phenotypes as a primary target for the next generation of preventive medicine.

documents.abstract: Against the background of global carbon neutrality goals and urban ecological transformation, traditional two-dimensional green-space indicators cannot fully reflect spatial–ecological benefits, and conventional 3D green-space calculation and landscape maintenance methods suffer from low accuracy and low efficiency. This paper proposes a theoretical technical framework combining multimodal remote sensing data, LiDAR point clouds and domain large language models for urban green-space scenarios. Firstly, a multimodal feature fusion strategy is constructed to adapt to complex urban environments, and a hierarchical calculation workflow for individual trees and regional 3D green-space is designed. Secondly, a full-life-cycle carbon accounting system for landscape engineering is established, which clarifies the accounting boundaries and quantitative methods of carbon sources and carbon sinks. Thirdly, a human–computer collaborative decision framework is proposed to realise intelligent recommendations for low-carbon maintenance schemes. This study focuses on theoretical framework construction and method exploration, and verifies the technical feasibility through simulation analysis. Different from existing independent research on green-space calculation or carbon accounting, this work integrates the two tasks and innovates a multimodal model application mode for landscape industry. This study focuses on theoretical framework construction and methodological exploration; feasibility assessment is only carried out via simulation deduction, rather than real-world field validation.

Time series forecasting increasingly exploits information that is not itself a numerical series, such as news text, imagery, contextual metadata, and relational structure among series. The term "multimodal" is nonetheless used without an operational definition, so that genuinely cross-modal models are pooled with multivariate and multi-view models that raise different problems. This paper proposes an operational criterion, together with a four-question procedure, that separates multimodal forecasting from multivariate, multi-view, and cross-modal model-reuse settings. On this basis it develops a five-axis taxonomy covering modality type, temporal alignment granularity, fusion mechanism, model family, and output form with uncertainty representation, and presents a structured synthesis of 33 published studies across eight application domains. Applying the criterion consistently shows that only 14 studies fully satisfy the definition. Notably, five large-language-model-based forecasters presented as series–text alignment methods use only text generated from the input series itself, which cannot add information about the future. Combined with published ablation evidence, this indicates that the benefit of an auxiliary modality is conditional rather than universal, and that evaluation practice, rather than architecture, is the binding constraint of the field. Generalisation under a shifting context–target relationship — the very condition auxiliary context is expected to address — remains essentially untested. The paper analyses seven groups of open challenges and proposes five research directions, notably multimodal self-supervised learning and offline semantic feature extraction with large language models, together with an eight-item minimum evaluation protocol intended to make the contribution of an auxiliary modality verifiable.

Learning rate schedules are typically fixed before training begins, yet when fine-tuning large language models with low-rank adapters (LoRA), the appropriate scale varies substantially with the model, task, and adapter configuration. Practitioners re-tune a schedule for every new problem, yet a tuned schedule still cannot react to the training dynamics it encounters. We instead amortize learning rate selection across LoRA fine-tuning problems. We leave the base optimizer, Muon, untouched, so that its normalized update fixes the direction, and meta-learn only the global step size. Our method MuPACE is a small recurrent policy, meta-trained across a distribution of fine-tuning runs, that conditions on the observed trajectory and emits bounded adjustments to an interpretable analytic schedule. On 64 fine-tuning problems, MuPACE outperforms standard fixed schedules at a strong shared default on 64-78% of problems and is on par with the same schedules with per-task tuned peaks. Meta-trained only on models with up to 16 layers, MuPACE transfers one-shot to unseen tasks on models as deep as 64 layers, such as Qwen3-32B and Qwen3.8-27B, where a single run remains competitive with swept schedules.

Generative artificial intelligence complicates a central problem in identifying musical giftedness: deciding which features of an outcome can reasonably be attributed to the student who presents it. A piece may display coherent formal design, an elaborate harmonic plan, idiomatic instrumentation, or convincing timbral balance even when those decisions were neither made nor understood by the learner. This conceptual article examines how music co-created with AI can be interpreted when the finished product no longer reveals the student’s contribution on its own. Drawing on research on musical talent development, AI-assisted creation, and assessment validity, it considers three sources of information: compositional problem framing, analytical listening and revision, and the traceability of musical decisions. Transfer across tasks provides a further check. These sources are not diagnostic criteria. They are intended to support more cautious interpretations of musical evidence in AI-mediated creative work and to complement broader developmental evidence used in identification processes.

ABSTRACT Recent progress in nanotechnology and biosensing is driving the development of advanced diagnostic tools for precision medicine. This review provides a systematic summary and critical analysis of intelligent nanobiosensors, which integrate engineered nanomaterials with biological recognition components and advanced signal‐transduction mechanisms. Key design paradigms, classification frameworks, and the role of diverse nanomaterials (e.g., metallic, carbon‐based, magnetic, and hybrid structures) are discussed in detail. Furthermore, major transduction technologies, including electrochemical, optical, mechanical, thermal, and magnetic platforms, together with clinical translation pathways and integration with artificial intelligence (AI), edge computing, and mobile health technologies, are comprehensively reviewed. Particular emphasis is placed on clinical applications in infectious, oncological, cardiovascular, and neurological diseases, as well as therapeutic monitoring. Key challenges, including scalability, data security, and regulatory barriers, are also critically discussed. Finally, emerging trends such as federated learning, the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), and personalized digital diagnostics are highlighted, providing perspectives on future directions in intelligent biosensing and precision healthcare.

Virtual docking and free-energy calculations can accelerate drug discovery, but practical use requires structural chemistry expertise, complex parameter selection and software integration. Here we show that iterative dialogue with an artificial intelligence (AI) coding assistant, OpenAI Codex, can guide a non-specialist scientist to build and operate a scripted, auditable computational workflow without direct coding. The assistant provided structural chemistry guidance and assembled an integrated pipeline for structure retrieval and preparation, binding-site definition, ligand preparation, virtual docking, interaction analysis, molecular dynamics (MD) and alchemical relative binding free-energy calculations. It also built a script generator for launching, monitoring and interpreting workflow runs. We tested the workflow on public cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2) benchmarks. After primary docking and multi-seed hit refinement, the active-ligand fraction increased from 1.73% in the input library to 80% in the ten-candidate handoff set (46.4-fold over input); a short MD stage acted as a structural quality-control gate on the leading candidates. Docking and hit refinement also generalized to human immunodeficiency virus reverse transcriptase and kinesin family member 11 benchmarks. In a CDK2 free-energy benchmark, the workflow achieved root-mean-square error = 0.66 kcal/mol and Pearson r = 0.90. Prompt-guided AI can orchestrate computational drug-discovery workflows for non-specialists while the underlying calculations remain the work of established external software and every run remains auditable.

Kids with autism, ADHD, or dyslexia hit roadblocks in regular schools their brains just work differently when it comes to focusing, thinking, or picking up new stuff at their own pace. That's why we built NeuroLearn AI: a web tool powered by smart tech that customizes lessons just for you, making school feel welcoming and doable. It keeps an eye on how you click, learn, and perform, then switches things up right away like easing the challenge level, changing how info shows up, or matching your best way to absorb it. You'll get helpers to stay on track, clean layouts that won't stress you out, game-like challenges to make it fun, and choices for seeing, hearing, or doing activities. All this ramps up what sticks in your head without overwhelming you, helps you learn on your own, and ditches that nagging school worry. Parents and teachers see updates as you go. Bottom line, NeuroLearn smooths out the bumps, making education fair for everyone—no matter how your mind ticks. Keywords: Neurodiversity, Adaptive Learning, Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), Personalized Education, Web Platform.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) and digitally mediated learning has intensified debate about flexibility, access, and quality assurance in higher education. This study examines stakeholder perceptions of the non-recognition of fully online doctoral education in India, focusing on career barriers, psychological burnout, acceptance of Education 4.0, institutional resistance, and support for policy reform. Using a cross-sectional questionnaire dataset of 832 respondents, the study applies descriptive statistics, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), group comparisons, and ordinary least squares (OLS) regression. The findings indicate comparatively high mean scores for perceived career barriers and Education 4.0 acceptance. Group comparisons did not identify statistically significant differences across the categories examined. The overall regression model was statistically significant (F(7, 824) = 64.28, p < 0.001; R² = 0.353; adjusted R² = 0.348). Institutional resistance was positively associated with policy-reform support, whereas career barriers showed a smaller negative association. Education 4.0 acceptance also showed a positive association with reform support. These findings represent statistical relationships within the sample and do not establish causal effects. The study contributes to discussions on Indian higher-education policy by outlining considerations for a quality-assured framework that addresses research supervision, assessment, academic integrity, institutional accountability, and equitable access to doctoral education.

Semantic data analytics systems integrate AI-powered operators into query pipelines, enabling declarative queries over structured and unstructured data. However, existing systems rely on per-tuple model invocations, ad hoc operator designs, and lack principled cost models, resulting in poor scalability and limited optimization. We present NousDB, a high-performance semantic analytics engine built on Apache DataFusion\cite{10.1145/3626246.3653368}.Through NousDB we propose an extended relational algebra with three semantic operators and formal algebraic properties that enable principled query rewriting and cross-operator optimization. We further propose a token-based cost model using equi-depth token histograms to optimize batch sizing under context-window constraints and provide statistical guarantees for safe batching. Experiments show that NousDB achieves up to $\times 86$ speedups with both local and enterprise LLMs, while leading competitors in token efficiency and accuracy. These gains extend to complex JOB and Stack workloads augmented with semantic operators, supporting both traditional and semantic analytics.

Healthcare systems produce and manage lots of highly sensitive information, especially in the form of prescriptions and other documents related to patients' private data. However, due to the nature of handwritten medical prescriptions and medical jargon, patients often find it difficult to follow medication instructions. Optical Character Recognition (OCR) is still in its nascent phase of digitizing handwritten prescription documents into text. Furthermore, the traditional OCR systems are noisy and difficult to understand when it comes to recognizing the handwriting of doctors to understand medical prescriptions properly. This paper utilizes Generative AI to test the ability of LLMs in conducting OCR on handwritten text and analyze its performance, and merge OCR with Generative AI to analyze and extract medicines from prescriptions in order to give a detailed and specialized description of the medicine to the user The paper further analyzes some OCR methods for text extraction from medical prescriptions and compares their performance. It has also been demonstrated that the usability of prescription data and the possibility of misinterpretation of medication is decreased when OCR is combined with Generative and Agentic AI. Thus the combination of artificial intelligence and OCR will help improve the understanding of patients and the accessibility of digital healthcare.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Purpose This study aims to develop an online method for reconstructing vision-based weld-seam coordinates corrupted by arc light, spatter and fumes, with the aim of providing stable coordinate inputs for robotic trajectory correction. Design/methodology/approach A RANSAC-based quadratic model is first used for robust small-sample initialization. Subsequent coordinates are processed using a coordinated-turn extended Kalman filter and Mahalanobis-distance outlier gating. The corrected points are then reconstructed by segment-wise cubic B-splines with endpoint and tangential-direction constraints. The method is evaluated using controlled outliers, naturally occurring welding disturbances, closed-loop TCP tracking, end-to-end latency and quantitative weld-quality measurements. Findings Under naturally occurring welding disturbances, the method achieved a precision of 95.14%, a recall of 93.84% and an F1 score of 94.49% for outlier identification. Coordinate RMSEs for straight, arc and S-curve paths were reduced to 0.31, 0.38 and 0.46 mm, respectively. Closed-loop TCP tracking RMSE decreased by 46.8%–48.7%, and the complete vision-to-control chain had an average latency of 60.5 ms for regular frames and 63.6 ms when B-spline smoothing was triggered, both below the 100 ms sampling period. Weld-width variation and centerline deviation were also reduced, whereas the change in spatter count was not statistically significant. Research limitations/implications The study is validated only on bead-on-plate welding of 5-mm Q235 steel at 10Hz visual sampling and 8mm/s speed, excluding assembled joints and multilayer welds. The constant-velocity Z-axis model may be inadequate for highly curved 3D seams. Future work should extend to adaptive noise estimation, higher speeds, complex spatial paths and real butt/fillet joints to generalize the framework. Practical implications The method reduces tool center point (TCP) tracking RMSE by ∼47% and improves weld-width consistency and centerline deviation, lowering rework and scrap costs. As a real-time add-on for existing robotic welding systems, it enables reliable automation under severe arc-light, spatter and fume disturbances. Its low latency (63.6ms) and modular architecture offer strong commercial potential for retrofitting industrial robots, attracting investment for cost-effective quality enhancement. Social implications Consistent weld quality reduces structural failures, enhancing public safety in infrastructure and manufacturing. Automating seam tracking decreases welders’ direct exposure to intense arc light, toxic fumes and high heat, improving occupational health. It also lowers skill entry barriers while creating higher-level supervisory and maintenance roles, fostering safer, more attractive working environments and supporting sustainable industrial development. Originality/value The contribution lies in a staged online architecture that integrates robust initialization, turn-rate state estimation, uncertainty-based outlier gating and finite-buffer smoothing for streaming weld coordinates. Its effectiveness is demonstrated not only at the coordinate level, but also through closed-loop robot motion, system-latency and weld-quality evaluation.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: Many scientific phenomena are best understood as outcomes of underlying optimization problems, yet automated scientific discovery has largely focused on recovering equations that describe observed input-output patterns. We introduce OptScientist, a novel automated framework for discovering compact symbolic optimization laws directly from data. OptScientist comprises (i) a model that infers symbolic optimization problems by first learning to represent data as an optimization problem and then extracting its symbolic form, and (ii) an LLM agentic system embedding the model in a discovery process that integrates theoretical priors from scientific literature, discovers candidate laws, abstracts their underlying mechanisms, and suggests new data to collect. We first evaluate OptScientist on OptFeynman, a novel benchmark of 99 physics-derived optimization problems, where OptScientist recovers ground-truth laws for over 80% of the problems and remains robust to noisy contextual information, while substantially outperforming machine-learning, symbolic, and LLM-based model-discovery baselines. On human risky choice and central-bank monetary policy, OptScientist discovers compact symbolic optimization laws that achieve held-out predictive performance competitive with leading baselines, while using few parameters and substantially fewer tokens than LLM baselines. Overall, OptScientist extends automated scientific discovery to uncovering optimization laws that generate observed phenomena, enabling automated theory building across the physical, biological, behavioral, and social sciences.

Juvenile systemic sclerosis (jSSc) is an orphan multisystem autoimmune disease that can cause significant morbidity during childhood and can lead to significant worsening of quality of life. The pathophysiological features are identical with adult-onset systemic sclerosis (SSc), jSSc exhibits a distinct clinical phenotype characterized by a significantly higher prevalence of diffuse cutaneous involvement, frequent overlap syndromes, distinct autoantibody profiles, and different long-term survival trajectories. Historically, the evaluation of jSSc has relied heavily on the extrapolation of adult outcome measures, which fail to account for developmental physiology, somatic growth, and pediatric-specific feasibility constraints. This review provides a comprehensive overview of indicators of disease activity and severity which might be used in daily clinical practice and adapted as outcome measures in future clinical trials. It includes global outcome measures, organ-specific outcomes (including skin, pulmonary, cardiac, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, renal, and vascular involvement), patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), and clinician-reported outcomes (ClinROs). The performance of adult indices within pediatric cohorts are evaluated, if applicable. Additionally, we analyze severity scores like the Juvenile Systemic Sclerosis Severity Score (J4S) alongside modern consensus metrics derived from the international Hamburg symposia. We emphasize the integration of pediatric-adapted clinical assessments, quantitative imaging, and patient and physician related outcomes. The development of outcome measure in jSSc requires a paradigm shift from static severity scores to dynamic, multi-dimensional indicators capable of differentiating reversible inflammatory activity from potential permanent damage accrual. Validating pediatric-specific thresholds for physiological and cutaneous change remains an urgent priority. Over the next decade, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven quantitative imaging, decentralized home-based digital health tools, and molecular biomarkers probably will gain an essential role to optimize clinical trial readiness and personalize therapeutic strategies for children with systemic sclerosis. Not applicable.

Examining existing benchmarks for grounding in 3D VLMs reveals a pervasive "semantic leakage" in the evaluation and prompting protocols: a heavy reliance on bounding boxes as spatial prompts or representation primitives. Because bounding boxes are highly informative of object categories, they introduce a shortcut for the models to neglect visual information during 3D VLM training. We demonstrate this with a "blind" LLM that, prompted only with the box coordinates, can perform surprisingly well. To further analyze this shortcut, we propose point-based grounding prompting - querying models with a single 3D point instead of a box. Under this protocol, the accuracy of the blind LLM drops from 36.4% to 18.0% on ScanNet's Nr3D, and similarly degrades for 3D VLMs (e.g. LL3DA). Building on this insight, we introduce P$^3$-VLM, a novel tri-pathway 3D VLM that supports point-based prompts and achieves 52.1% state-of-the-art accuracy on location-grounded captioning under this setting. To achieve this, we redesign the architecture while keeping it detector-free, scene-centric, and suitable for 3D GS inputs. P$^3$-VLM utilizes three complementary pathways (location-, task-, and context-aware), enabling strong reasoning about scenes without any bounding box dependencies. The key benefit of point-based learning is a consistent improvement across settings: P$^3$-VLM achieves state-of-the-art performance under point-based grounding while also improving robustness, OOD generalization, and performance on ungrounded scene-centric 3D VQA benchmarks, reflecting its reduced reliance on bounding-box shortcuts and resulting stronger visual-spatial reasoning.

Induction machines have a broad array of applications in various fields, from transport to healthcare. It is necessary to know the equivalent circuit parameters to determine the behavior of these machines under different load conditions and to control the speed position. Equivalent circuit parameters can be obtained experimentally using the IEEE 112 standard. In addition, the artificial intelligence models demonstrate a capacity for highly precise estimation of the parameters based on the data obtained from the machine manufacturers instead of using approximation formulas. In the study, the equivalent circuit parameters of squirrel-cage induction motors with different power ratings were estimated for single and double-cage models using the XGBoost algorithm with metaheuristic optimization. The proposed method has been scrutinized with the existing studies for both models and its performance has been studied. With the proposed algorithm, more successful results were obtained for the single-cage model than other algorithms. Furthermore, the results obtained for the double-cage model are competitive with other methods. In this study, the Particle Swarm optimization algorithm, a well-known metaheuristic optimization algorithm, is applied to determine the optimal configuration of the Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) algorithm to improve the prediction accuracy of the Machine Learning (ML) model. The results clearly show that the proposed approach is better than the existing literature. The performances of the proposed approach on the single and double cages are obtained with Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) values of 1.79% and 6.36%, respectively.

Smartphones are now embedded in family, educational, and occupational routines, yet their interpersonal costs are not adequately captured by screen-time measures alone. This conceptual article examines parental smartphone phubbing during school-related parent-child interactions and develops an integrated developmental explanation of how repeated attentional interruptions may become educationally meaningful. Drawing on a critical interpretive and integrative synthesis of scholarship on digital parenting, technoference, attachment, emotion regulation, academic engagement, self-determination, bioecological development, and family systems, the article positions caregiver responsiveness as the proximal mechanism connecting parental digital distraction with children's developmental experiences. The proposed framework suggests a sequence in which recurrent parental phubbing may reduce perceived caregiver responsiveness, contribute to less secure expectations of caregiver availability, constrain opportunities for interpersonal co-regulation, and, in turn, weaken behavioural, emotional, and cognitive engagement with learning. The model does not treat smartphones as inherently harmful and does not claim empirically established causality. Instead, it identifies relational interruption, developmental accumulation, and contextual moderation as the conditions under which device use may acquire psychological significance. School-related interactions are highlighted as a distinctive context because homework, examination preparation, academic problem solving, and discussions of school experiences simultaneously involve cognitive scaffolding and emotional support. The framework integrates six complementary theoretical traditions and extends prior work by linking family digital behaviour to educational engagement through a coherent developmental cascade. Implications are developed for research design, parent education, school counselling, educational psychology, and culturally responsive work in India. A staged agenda for longitudinal, dyadic, observational, and intervention research is proposed to test the model.

This study aims to examine the extent to which the intensity of face-to-face group discussions within the deep learning approach contributes to the cognitive engagement of eighth-grade students at SMPN 1 Kebonagung. This study employed a quantitative approach with a causal-associative research design. The research population consisted of 96 students from three classes, namely VIII D, VIII E, and VIII F. However, only 85 students completed all stages of data collection and were therefore determined as the research sample. The independent variable, namely group discussion intensity, was measured using a Likert-scale questionnaire, while the dependent variable, namely cognitive engagement, was measured using teacher observation sheets and peer assessment. Data were analyzed using SPSS version 26, including descriptive statistics, normality testing, linearity testing, and simple linear regression analysis. The findings indicate that group discussion intensity has a positive and significant effect on students' cognitive engagement, as indicated by a significance value of 0.048, which is below 0.05. The coefficient of determination (R²) of 0.336 indicates that group discussion intensity accounts for 33.6% of the variation in students' cognitive engagement, while the remaining 66. Other variables beyond the scope of this study influence 4%. In conclusion, the more intensive the group discussions during learning, the higher the students' level of cognitive engagement.

The rise of digital technology has helped the modernization of the tax system through Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digital-based tax services. Generation Z, as a cohort that has grown up in the digital era, is expected to adapt to these advances which would improve tax compliance. The present study intends to assess the influence of the application of Artificial Intelligence in taxes and digital literacy on the compliance of Generation Z taxpayers through a systematic literature review approach. The research strategy employed is the Systematic Literature Review (SLR) by assessing five relevant scientific articles published in the year 2022-2026. The results of the study reveal that there has not been a consistent direct effect of AI and tax digitization on taxpayer compliance. Conversely, digital literacy has been identified as a critical factor to improve taxpayers’ awareness, access and utilization of digital tax services. Tax literacy and tax socialization are other supporting elements that increase the relationship between tax technology and taxpayer compliance. These results demonstrate that the effective adoption of AI in taxation is not only based on the technological sophistication but also on the level of digital literacy and tax understanding of users. Thus, there is a need for a strategy that include technology advancement, greater digital literacy, and tax education to promote sustainable compliance among Generation Z taxpayers.

The rapid development of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed learning and working paradigms, shifting the primary challenge from merely seeking information to the ability to formulate precise instructions (prompting). Despite high technology access in Senior High Schools (SMA), its utilization remains largely superficial. This research aims to enhance students' AI literacy skills—encompassing conceptual understanding, ethical awareness, and information verification—through structured prompt engineering training. The study employed a quantitative approach with a pre-experimental one-group pretest–posttest design involving 31 students at SMA 1 Sedayu, Bantul, Yogyakarta. The intervention was delivered through training based on the Role–Task–Context (RTC) framework and hands-on practice using mobile devices. Data analysis included normality tests (Shapiro-Wilk and Kolmogorov-Smirnov), Spearman correlation, and paired samples t-tests. The results indicated a significant increase in mean scores, rising from 57.10 in the pre-test to 89.68 in the post-test. Statistically, |t-Stat| (18.16) > t-Critical (2.04) with a significance value of (p < 0.05), leading to the acceptance of the alternative hypothesis (H_1). A strong Pearson correlation (0.759) demonstrated students' consistency in adopting new techniques. The training successfully transitioned students from passive technology consumers to proactive information managers. In conclusion, integrating prompt engineering as a life skill can transform students' digital behavior from mere entertainment into sophisticated productivity tools, while simultaneously strengthening digital literacy in the digital creative economy era.

Kegiatan Pengabdian kepada Masyarakat (PkM) ini bertujuan untuk meningkatkan kreativitas digital siswa melalui pemanfaatan Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) berbasis cloud computing di SMK Ikhlas Jawilan. Pelatihan difokuskan pada pengenalan konsep dasar Artificial Intelligence, Generative AI, dan cloud computing, serta praktik pemanfaatan platform PartyRock dalam menghasilkan aplikasi sederhana dan konten visual berbasis AI. Metode pelaksanaan menggunakan pendekatan experiential learning sehingga peserta memperoleh pengalaman belajar secara langsung dalam mengembangkan karya digital. Evaluasi kegiatan dilakukan melalui pengukuran pada tahap pra dan pasca pelatihan terhadap indikator partisipasi peserta, pemahaman AI dan cloud computing, kemampuan praktik, kreativitas digital, kepercayaan diri, kolaborasi, respons sekolah, serta keberlanjutan pemanfaatan teknologi. Hasil evaluasi menunjukkan bahwa seluruh indikator mengalami peningkatan setelah pelatihan, dengan nilai rata-rata meningkat dari 77,88% pada tahap pra pelatihan menjadi 91,13% pada tahap pasca pelatihan. Capaian pasca pelatihan berada pada kisaran 88-95%, yang menunjukkan peningkatan pada aspek pengetahuan, keterampilan, dan sikap peserta dalam memanfaatkan Generative AI. Hasil tersebut menunjukkan bahwa pelatihan berhasil meningkatkan pemahaman, keterampilan kreativitas digital serta kesiapan peserta dalam memanfaatkan teknologi AI secara produktif dan bertanggung jawab. Selain memberikan manfaat bagi siswa, kegiatan ini juga membantu guru dalam memperluas wawasan terkait pemanfaatan teknologi AI sebagai media pendukung pembelajaran yang inovatif dan adaptif terhadap perkembangan teknologi modern. Secara keseluruhan, kegiatan PkM ini berkontribusi positif dan memiliki potensi untuk dikembangkan sebagai program pelatihan berkelanjutan guna memperkuat literasi digital, mendorong inovasi pembelajaran, serta mengoptimalkan pemanfaatan teknologi Generative AI di lingkungan sekolah.

Citizens’ social media posts can provide rapid, complementary situational information during emerging wildfires, alongside conventional sensing and official reporting. For Greek, no annotated wildfire corpus or end-to-end pipeline existed, and most systems stop at binary detection or depend on geotags. We present an end-to-end Greek-language NLP pipeline, a research prototype that turns keyword-retrieved, unlabeled X posts into a geolocated, near-real-time wildfire map: it detects active fires, types them as wildland, urban, or mixed, resolves toponyms, and clusters reports into incidents. On 3277 manually annotated posts from two fire seasons, the first publicly released, agreement-audited Greek wildfire corpus to our knowledge, fine-tuned transformers reached F2 = 0.911 for detection and macro-F1 = 0.874 for fire type, outperforming classical baselines and, under the tested prompting conditions, two large language models, while being faster and free of API costs. On a chronological hold-out of the unseen 2025 season, detection retains F2 = 0.850 (classification recall 0.907); fire-type classification degrades more (macro-F1 0.769 ± 0.085). Spatiotemporal toponym disambiguation raised geocoding accuracy from 54.68% to 80.58% (p < 0.001); a repeatability test revealed gazetteer drift. In a retrospective replay of 12 August 2024 posts, it resolved hundreds of reports of an Attica wildfire into one incident cluster, complementing emergency calls.

In the last 250 years, Mankind has gone through 4 Industrial Revolutions, namely Industries 1.0 to Industry 4.0, in which innovative science, technology and novel materials have played a definitive role. Despite that a great part of Humanity is just entering Industry 4.0 (namely, cyberspace, artificial intelligence, robotics, cloud computing, etc.) a new Industrial revolution is emerging: Industry 5.0 in which all the current and future technologies must be aligned with human development, if a truly sustainable world is to be achieved. In this Perspective, a discussion on the main characteristics of each of the 4 Industrial Revolutions is presented, along with a reflection on the upcoming Industry 5.0, which will certainly be at the very center of the stockholders: novel materials, the need for sustainability and the role of humans, which requires a truly Global Ethics if a truly inclusive 5.0 Revolution is to be achieved.
